slides.title: A Story - Family stories, in the voices that lived them.
slides.spoken: Hi, we’re A Story. We build an AI biographer that calls your loved ones and helps them tell their stories in their own voice - and lets the whole family add their part. Today I’ll show you why families keep losing these stories, what we built, what’s already working, and the proof we’re going after next. A Story is a member of NVIDIA Inception, the AssemblyAI Startup Program, and a Cartesia Startups Grant recipient.

slides.title: Eighty years of a life, remembered by two dates and a folder of photos
slides.spoken: A person can live for eighty years and eventually be remembered by a birth date, a death date, and a folder of photographs. Everything in between - what they chose, believed, regretted, and loved - is never written down. Dates and photographs can prove that someone lived, but their stories are what allow us to know who they were. When those stories fade, we lose them a second time.

slides.title: Think about how your parents met
slides.spoken: Think about how your parents met. You probably know the short version - they met at a dance. But do you know what almost kept them apart, or how each of them remembers that day? Mom and Dad may not even agree about who made the first move.

slides.title: Every retelling loses a little more
slides.spoken: That is how family stories work. They pass by word of mouth: one person remembers one part, someone else remembers another, so no one carries the whole story. With each retelling, details shift - the Elks Hall dance becomes “a dance in Toledo, I think,” then “a party?”, then nothing. If someone never passes their part on, no one else can recover it.

slides.title: never-forget
slides.spoken: Every family has an “I’ll never forget this day” story. Even that one can be lost if no one else ever hears it. That is the legacy gap.

slides.title: For adult children, this is not a niche problem
slides.spoken: For adult children, this is not a niche problem. 79% want to know more about their parents’ lives before parenthood, but only 37% know their mother’s life before she became a parent - most of her story before you is a part no one asked about. And 74% regret not learning more about relatives who have died, when it’s too late to ask.

slides.title: Wanting to know isn’t the same as finding the moment to ask
slides.spoken: Wanting to know is not the same as finding the right moment to ask. Questions rarely arrive at a convenient time. You think of one at midnight, your parent is asleep three time zones away, and by the next call, the question is gone. Families care - they just keep missing the moment.

slides.title: why-not-ask
slides.spoken: Life happens. You can’t sustainably find time every day to get to know your parents, and some nights you just need to hear their voice, for comfort. Just imagine being one click away from their voice and stories, anywhere, any time. You may not always have the time to call them, but you shouldn’t have to wait for the perfect moment to feel close to them.

slides.title: They keep pieces, not the story
slides.spoken: Most current options fall into two categories: photo albums and memoir services. Albums keep the pictures, but lose the life behind them. Memoir services, like Storyworth, try to solve this with weekly prompts toward a physical keepsake. But what’s supposed to be a meaningful gift turns out to be homework for the parents. Habit research found a median of 66 days of daily repetition; weekly prompts allow only about ten attempts in that time, and many only move forward the first few before abandoning as life gets busy. And once the book is printed, the purpose is gone. The book ends. The everyday doesn’t - and that’s where most of a life’s stories happen.

slides.title: blank-page
slides.spoken: Most people will never write an autobiography. No one can recall a whole life at once - eighty years don’t fit on a blank page. But anyone can tell one story tonight.

slides.title: Meet A Story: an AI biographer that calls your loved ones
slides.spoken: Most people will never write an autobiography - not because their lives are empty, but because reconstructing a whole life from a blank page is an overwhelming place to begin. Meet A Story, an AI biographer that calls your loved ones and helps them tell their stories in their own voice. The phone rings at the time they picked. They answer and talk; A Story does the asking, listens to what they actually say, and follows the conversation instead of a fixed script. After each call, A Story keeps the original voice and transcript and turns what was shared into a memory the family can revisit, connected to the photos, letters, people and dates around it. The interviewer remembers what has already been shared, picks up unfinished stories, and lets each memory shape the next conversation - a life preserved gradually, while it’s still being lived. (Live today: calls, archive, photo uploads and billing. The home screen shows Rose, the example family in the app.)

slides.title: Rome wasn’t built in one day. Or by one person.
slides.spoken: Rome wasn’t built in one day - or by one person. One person can only tell the part they remember, so A Story is collaborative: every narrator can be in the room. Rose tells the summer at the lake on her call. Her daughter Jamie adds three photos of the dock. Uncle John adds his own version of the race. And the next time A Story calls Rose, it asks about what the family added. The original conversation stays at the center, and every account is kept side by side and credited - never merged into one “official” version. A photograph can raise a question no one thought to ask, and a missing detail can go to the relative most likely to know it. What begins as one person’s autobiography grows into a documentary of their life. (Rose’s family is the example family in the app screens. Relatives’ input shaping the next call is our core design and the thing we’re measuring now.)

slides.title: It never assumes the story is finished. Today is part of it too.
slides.spoken: This is what makes A Story more than an app for interviewing grandparents. Other tools look backward - a memoir to finish before it’s too late. A Story never assumes the story is finished. Today is part of it too. The same model works for a grandparent’s whole life; for new parents capturing first words and the ordinary days childhood leaves behind; for a wedding told by everyone who was there; for a reunion, remembered by everyone at the table; for any ordinary day. Mom and Dad can start their child’s story today, so one day their child can return to those years through their parents’ eyes and voices. And when the family wants something physical, any chapter becomes a printed book - a chapter, not the finish line. A family tree brought to life.

slides.title: Other products end with a book. A Story becomes a habit.
slides.spoken: This is the core of how we think about it. Other products are projects with an ending: prompts, a book, done. A Story is a habit. The phone rings at the time they chose, and they just answer - no homework. Every call, every photo, every relative’s version adds to the same living memory. A printed book is one chapter along the way, not the finish line. The story is never finished; today is part of it too.

slides.title: America is aging - and families live further apart
slides.spoken: And it can’t wait. America is aging: 11,200 Americans turn 65 every day through 2027 - about 467 an hour, roughly 8 a minute - and by 2030 every baby boomer will be 65 or older. Nearly 1 in 5 Americans is already 65+, 64.6 million people. At the same time, families live further apart. And $124 trillion will pass between generations through 2048. Families plan carefully how to pass on their money. Who’s planning how to pass on their stories? The stories that used to come up at Sunday dinner now need a reason - and a way - to be told.

slides.title: Now it’s affordable, familiar and one call away
slides.spoken: Families have always wanted these stories. What changed is that ongoing interviews are now affordable, familiar and one call away. Affordable: after the 2026 voice price cuts - text-to-speech down up to 55% - the same dollar buys about 2.2 times as much voice (1 ÷ 0.45), and a 7–10 minute interview costs about $0.32–0.45 on our stack, modeled. Familiar: generative-AI use among adults 50+ went from 9% in 2023 to 30% in 2025 - 3.3 times in two years. One call away: 95% of adults 65+ own a cellphone. There is no app to learn; after setup, they just answer a scheduled call.

slides.title: Built with families. Ready to prove retention.
slides.spoken: The core product already works end to end: scheduled AI-guided phone interviews, transcripts and the family archive, relative invitations and photo contributions, and billing. We’re in private beta on TestFlight, and our App Store release is in review. Our first MVP brought in 50 leads. We deliberately selected 10 families for the private beta, learned from their actual behavior, and redesigned the product before scaling - and another five are waiting to join as paying customers at the redesigned release. Hope College has shown interest in gifting A Story to students’ grandparents this holiday season - interest, not a signed partnership. We’re members of NVIDIA Inception and the AssemblyAI Startup Program, and recipients of a Cartesia Startups Grant. What we measure next is what matters most: whether storytellers come back for another call, whether relatives contribute, and whether those contributions create the next conversation. (All traction is owner-reported; no payment records yet.)

slides.title: Families pay to keep the story growing
slides.spoken: How we make money. First, subscription, because that is what keeps the story growing: families pay yearly for the ongoing interviews - $119 for an individual, with one storyteller, 90 minutes of calls a month and a Classic Hardcover each year; or $229 for a family plan, with up to three storytellers and 200 shared minutes a month. Relatives read and contribute for free. There’s also a one-time Express gift pass at $79 and a $19.99 monthly plan. Second, books, whenever the family wants something physical - softcover from $39, Classic Hardcover $69, Heirloom $149. The book is a chapter, not the finish line. It’s bought as a gift, but kept as a habit: the adult child buys, the parent just answers the phone, and every relative who adds a memory gives the next call - and the next year - a reason. Renewal is the number we are proving next.

slides.title: A national market, starting with 65+ households
slides.spoken: Bottom-up. 132.7 million U.S. households at our $119 price is a $15.8 billion ceiling. We start with the 43.6 million households that include someone 65 or older: $5.19 billion a year. And the target that matters: at about $141 per account - an 80/20 mix of Individual and Family plans - roughly 710,000 paying accounts, just 1.6% of 65+ households, is a $100 million a year business. These are demographic ceilings, not validated demand; one paid account covers a whole family.

slides.title: Guided calls exist. We win on the family workflow.
slides.spoken: Guided calls already exist, and we respect that. Storyworth advertises Story Calls with follow-ups and Family Calls that keep two voices. Remento lets collaborators add questions, photos and their own stories. Storii schedules up to three calls a week. Spomen does follow-ups and multiple perspectives. So phone calls and family contributions are becoming category features. Where we win is the family workflow: scheduled calls that come to the storyteller, every relative’s version kept side by side and credited, and what relatives add shaping the next call - so the story keeps going after the first year instead of ending with the book. That last piece is our core design and what we’re measuring now, not a proven edge yet. “Not stated” means the company’s public pages don’t say either way.

slides.title: Launch for the holidays. Then prove they come back.
slides.spoken: Our next step is the public launch and the holiday gifting campaign. First, convert the five families already waiting - our first paying customers on the redesigned release. Second, launch into the gifting season: the App Store release, gift passes for adult children, and a first partner gifting campaign with Hope College, who have shown interest. Third, prove that families come back: storytellers returning for another call, relatives contributing, and what they add shaping the next question. The path to our first hundred is channel math, not market share - for example, 1,000 qualified visits at 3% who buy and stay is 30 paying families. Those are example inputs; we’ll replace them with measured conversion. We’ll report back on second-call rate, relatives contributing, calls that use family input, and real cost per call against our model.

slides.title: Two full-time founders, based in Michigan
slides.spoken: We are two full-time founders based in Michigan, and we bring two different reasons to believe we will make this work. I’m Bao Vo, COO. I run operations, customer discovery and partnerships, and I chose our ten beta families from fifty leads. Before A Story I built go-to-market strategy for three early-stage biotech startups at miLEAD Consulting, and as an engineer I taped out a 22nm chip on a 1.5-month deadline at Faraday Technology, with a top-10% evaluation. I was a fully funded ECE doctoral fellow at the University of Michigan. Daniel Hoang Nguyen, our CEO, lived the problem: the two uncles who carried his family’s history had strokes and struggled to find the words. He ranked first at BGSU in the Putnam Competition, is Phi Beta Kappa, placed second at the 2025 BGSU Hackathon for an AI search framework, and leads product vision, fundraising and finance. One founder who lived the problem, one who builds go-to-market for early ventures. We met in 2024 through the Vietnamese student community, and we’re a Delaware C-Corp based in Allendale, Michigan. (For the Michigan Business Challenge edition, Pitch Tailor adds Nhi Tran, CMO.)

slides.title: close
slides.spoken: We’ve built the product. Now we’re proving that preserving a life story can become something families continue - not another project they start and abandon - so that “I meant to ask” doesn’t become “I wish I had.” Thank you. [Program editions add their ask on the slide before this one: the amount and the one result it funds.]

slides.title: The model has to work when families actually use it
slides.spoken: Modeled, not observed. First-year contribution per account, before acquisition and fixed costs: $77 at 25% of minutes used, $61 at 50%, $28 at 100% on our component voice stack. On a managed-agent stack it’s $53, $13 and a loss of $69 - so full use on a managed stack doesn’t work at today’s prices. At 50% use, out of $141: $8.79 payment fees, $32.74 voice, $14.40 hosting, $18 support, $6 archive reserve, about $37 acquisition plus trial, leaving $24.12 before fixed costs. At full use that turns to about minus $8.61. Assumptions: 80% Individual / 20% Family plan mix; 2026 voice pricing.
